unit_name: Medieval England: the Reign of Edward I, 1272-1307
key_individuals_and_groups: Edward I — king of England 1272-1307, the depth-study protagonist; legal reformer, conqueror of Wales, would-be conqueror of Scotland.
Henry III — Edward's father, whose troubled reign (Provisions of Oxford, Second Barons' War) shaped Edward's determination to restore royal authority.
Eleanor of Castile — Edward's queen, accompanied him on campaign and to Caernarfon for the birth of their heir in 1284; her death in 1290 prompted the Eleanor Crosses.
Robert Burnell — Lord Chancellor 1274-1292, architect of the Hundred Rolls inquiry and the great Edwardian statutes.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd — Prince of Wales, whose refusal to pay homage triggered the war of 1277 and the war of 1282-83 in which he was killed at Cilmeri.
Dafydd ap Gruffudd — Llywelyn's brother, whose 1282 attack on Hawarden Castle reignited the Welsh war; first nobleman in England executed by hanging, drawing and quartering, 1283.
Master James of St George — Savoyard master of works for Edward's Welsh castle programme; designer (or supervising architect) of Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris.
Madog ap Llywelyn — leader of the Welsh revolt of 1294-95 that briefly captured Caernarfon's unfinished works.
John Balliol — chosen king of Scots 1292 in the Great Cause; deposed by Edward 1296 after the sack of Berwick.
Robert Bruce (the elder, the Competitor; and his grandson Robert Bruce the future Robert I) — Balliol's rivals in the Great Cause; the younger Bruce would resume the war against Edward I in 1306.
William Wallace — leader of Scottish resistance from 1297; victor at Stirling Bridge 1297, defeated at Falkirk 1298, executed 1305.
Roger Bacon and Duns Scotus — Franciscan scholars symbolising thirteenth-century English learning and the medieval universities (Oxford).
The Italian bankers — the Riccardi of Lucca financed the Welsh wars until 1294; the Frescobaldi of Florence took over royal lending after the Riccardi collapse.
The expelled Jewish community of England — c.2,000-3,000 Jews expelled by royal edict 18 July 1290 after generations of legal discrimination and forced conversion campaigns.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students often write that the 1295 'Model Parliament' was an elected representative body in the modern sense. In reality every parliament under Edward was summoned by the king for his own purposes — typically to grant taxation or hear judicial business — and the 'commons' element (knights of the shire and burgesses) was widened so the king could raise money more efficiently, not because of a constitutional principle.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option B and Pearson/Hodder GCSE History textbooks for the 8145 Edward I option.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat the famous 'Hammer of the Scots' label as a contemporary judgement that Edward had crushed Scotland by 1307. The phrase comes from the inscription on Edward's tomb at Westminster (added later, possibly in the sixteenth century) and Edward died on the way to a fresh Scottish campaign with Robert Bruce already crowned and resistance very much alive.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Marc Morris, A Great and Terrible King: Edward I and the Forging of Britain (2008); Westminster Abbey tomb inscription scholarship.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the two Welsh wars (1277 and 1282-83) with the Scottish wars from 1296 onwards, blurring a fifteen-year gap. Wales is largely settled by the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284; Scottish involvement only begins seriously with the Great Cause of 1290-92.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports flagging chronological confusion across British depth study options.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students frame the expulsion either as a sudden act of personal antisemitism or as purely a financial decision. It was both — a deeply rooted cultural antisemitism reinforced by ritual-murder libels and the 1275 Statute of the Jewry, combined with the political opportunity to extract a parliamentary grant of £116,000 from a grateful tax-paying public in exchange for the edict.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Robin R. Mundill, England's Jewish Solution (1998); History Today scholarship on the 1290 expulsion.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Edward I, Edward II and Edward III
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the three Edwards — attributing the loss at Bannockburn (1314, Edward II) or victories of the Hundred Years War (Edward III) to Edward I. The depth study covers only 1272-1307; Bannockburn is seven years after Edward I's death.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B and standard GCSE textbook errata.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe Caernarfon as a military fortress only, missing the deliberate triple function of fortress, palace and walled colonial town. The polygonal towers and banded masonry were chosen to broadcast imperial Roman/Constantinopolitan symbolism — its purpose was as much ideological as defensive.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Cadw (Welsh Government heritage agency) Caernarfon Castle official guide and UNESCO World Heritage nomination dossier for the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 16-mark historic environment essay, top-band answers explicitly connect features of Caernarfon Castle (e.g. polygonal towers, banded masonry, the planted borough) to wider events of Edward's reign such as the Statute of Rhuddlan, the second Welsh war, the wool tax, or the 1294 Madog revolt — describing the castle in isolation will lose marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B and AQA examiner commentary on historic environment questions.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 'describe two features' (4 marks), examiners want two clearly separate features each given a supporting detail — students who give one elaborate feature lose half the marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B 'describe two features' questions across multiple series.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 'explain why' / 'explain effects' (8 marks), the highest band requires causal links between events — 'X caused Y because...' — not a parallel list of factors. For Edward I this means treating the Welsh wars, the wool tax, the bankers and the castle programme as a connected system rather than separate topics.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B 8-mark questions.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Students who deploy precise medieval terminology (statute, writ, chancery, exchequer, borough, demesne, bailiff, escheator, eyre, marcher lordship) cluster in higher bands — vague language ('the king made a law') caps marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA SPaG performance descriptors (spec section 4.4.3) and examiner reports on candidates' use of specialist vocabulary.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Historiographical awareness — even brief contrast between Marc Morris's view of Edward as a 'great and terrible king' and Michael Prestwich's emphasis on administrative achievement — lifts conclusions on the 16-mark question.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: Marc Morris, A Great and Terrible King (2008) and Michael Prestwich, Edward I (Yale English Monarchs series, rev. 1997); standard A-level transition reading lists.

historiography_notes.view: Edward as efficient administrator and law-giver
historiography_notes.supporting_scholarship: Michael Prestwich's Edward I (Yale English Monarchs, rev. 1997) emphasises the Hundred Rolls inquiry, the Statutes of Westminster (1275, 1285), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279), the Quo Warranto inquiries and the development of parliament as administrative achievements that shaped English government for centuries.

Marc Morris's A Great and Terrible King (2008) and revisionist Welsh and Scottish historians stress the violence of the 1282-83 Welsh war (Llywelyn's killing at Cilmeri, Dafydd's hanging-drawing-and-quartering), the colonial planted boroughs, the 1290 expulsion of the Jews, and the savagery at Berwick in 1296.

Older 'Whig' tradition (Stubbs, Tout) viewed the 1295 Model Parliament as a step towards parliamentary democracy; modern scholarship (David Carpenter, John Maddicott) shows Edward's parliaments were instruments for raising tax and dispensing justice — but the broadened summons did establish a precedent that later kings could not easily reverse.

lessons.title: Edward's Inheritance: From Henry III to a New King
lessons.description: Edward I's accession in 1272, Henry III's troubled legacy and the problems facing the new king.
lessons.spec_part: Part 1 — Government, the rights of King and people
spec_bullets_covered: Henry III's legacy and Edward's relationship with his father
lessons.lesson_focus: Why Edward inherited a damaged crown — the Provisions of Oxford 1258, the Second Barons' War, Simon de Montfort's parliament 1265, the Battle of Evesham, and Edward's Crusade absence on his accession in November 1272.

lessons.title: Restoring Royal Authority: The Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto
lessons.description: Edward's first inquiry into the state of the kingdom and his challenge to noble privilege.
lessons.spec_part: Part 1 — Government, the rights of King and people
lessons.lesson_focus: The 1274-75 Hundred Rolls survey, Robert Burnell as Lord Chancellor, the Quo Warranto inquiries from 1278 ('By what warrant?') challenging baronial liberties, and the limits Edward met when nobles produced 'rusty swords' as proof of ancient right.

lessons.title: Edward the Lawgiver: The Statutes of Westminster, Gloucester and Mortmain
lessons.description: The great Edwardian statutes that reshaped land law, justice and the church.
lessons.spec_part: Part 1 — Government, the rights of King and people
spec_bullets_covered: Development of government, rights and justice
lessons.lesson_focus: First Statute of Westminster 1275, Statute of Gloucester 1278, Statute of Mortmain 1279 (limiting grants of land to the church), Second Statute of Westminster 1285 with the doctrine 'De Donis Conditionalibus', and Statute of Winchester 1285 reforming local policing.

lessons.title: Wool, Banks and the Royal Purse
lessons.description: How agriculture, the wool trade and Italian bankers funded Edward's ambitions.
lessons.lesson_focus: England as the wool exporter of Europe, the 'Maltolt' wool customs from 1275 and 1294, the Riccardi of Lucca financing the first Welsh war, the Frescobaldi taking over after the Riccardi collapse in 1294, the great re-coinage of 1279-80, and the Statute of Merchants 1285 protecting creditors.

lessons.title: Crime, Courts and Punishment in Edward's England
lessons.description: How royal justice reached every village through courts, juries and brutal punishments.
spec_bullets_covered: The development of the legal system: laws; courts; trials; crimes; criminals and punishments
lessons.lesson_focus: The royal courts (King's Bench, Common Pleas, Exchequer of Pleas), the eyre and the assize justices on circuit, trial by jury replacing trial by ordeal, Statute of Winchester 1285 organising the hue and cry and the watch, and the visible spectacle of medieval punishment (hanging, the pillory, hanging-drawing-and-quartering of Dafydd ap Gruffudd 1283).

lessons.title: Faith and Learning: The Church, Universities and Roger Bacon
lessons.description: The thirteenth-century church, the rise of Oxford and Cambridge, and the intellectual life of medieval England.
spec_bullets_covered: Education and learning: the medieval Church, universities, Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus
lessons.lesson_focus: The friars (Franciscans and Dominicans) bringing new scholarship, Roger Bacon's experimental science and his Opus Majus, Duns Scotus and the 'subtle doctor', the rise of Oxford colleges (Balliol, Merton, University) and Cambridge, and tensions between papal authority and Edward's crown.

lessons.title: The Expulsion of the Jews, 1290
lessons.description: The Statute of the Jewry, mounting persecution and Edward's edict expelling England's Jewish community.
lessons.lesson_focus: The Jewish community in thirteenth-century England, the Statute of the Jewry 1275 forcing Jews out of moneylending, the ritual-murder libels (Hugh of Lincoln 1255), the parliamentary tax bargain of 1290, the Edict of Expulsion of 18 July 1290, and the long aftermath until readmission under Cromwell in 1656.

lessons.title: Medieval Warfare: Cavalry, Castles and Crossbows
lessons.description: The tactics, weapons and technology of late thirteenth-century warfare.
lessons.spec_part: Part 3 — Edward I's military campaigns in Wales and Scotland
spec_bullets_covered: Medieval warfare, tactics and technology: siege warfare, battlefield use of cavalry, infantry, weapons and armour
lessons.lesson_focus: The composition of an Edwardian army (knights, men-at-arms, longbow archers from south Wales and Cheshire, crossbowmen, foot-soldiers), siege warfare technology (mangonel, trebuchet, scaling, sapping, mining), the rise of plate over mail, and the cost of equipping a knight versus a foot-soldier.

lessons.title: Conquering Wales: The Wars of 1277 and 1282-83
lessons.description: From Llywelyn's defiance to the death of the last native Prince of Wales and the Statute of Rhuddlan.
lessons.spec_part: Part 3 — Edward I's military campaigns in Wales and Scotland
spec_bullets_covered: The invasion and colonisation of Wales
lessons.lesson_focus: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd's refusal to pay homage 1274-76, the first war 1277 ending in the Treaty of Aberconwy, Dafydd ap Gruffudd's attack on Hawarden Castle 1282 reigniting war, Llywelyn's death at Cilmeri December 1282, Dafydd's execution as the first English nobleman to be hanged-drawn-and-quartered 1283, and the Statute of Rhuddlan 1284 imposing English shire administration on Gwynedd.
lessons.absorbed_from_dropped_lesson: Also covers the Iron Ring castle programme as the post-conquest settlement: Beaumaris, Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech as instruments of Plantagenet control, polygonal towers, Master James of St George's designs, the £25,000 build cost. Treat castles as a class of structure, not as the rotating historic environment site.

lessons.title: The Great Cause and the Conquest of Scotland, 1290-1296
lessons.description: Edward as overlord — the disputed Scottish succession, John Balliol's brief reign and the sack of Berwick.
lessons.spec_part: Part 3 — Edward I's military campaigns in Wales and Scotland
lessons.lesson_focus: The death of Alexander III 1286 and the Maid of Norway 1290, Edward as the chosen arbiter in the Great Cause 1291-92, John Balliol crowned 1292, the auld alliance with France 1295, Edward's invasion of 1296 with the brutal sack of Berwick, the deposition of Balliol ('Toom Tabard'), and the removal of the Stone of Scone to Westminster.

lessons.title: Wallace, Bruce and the 'Hammer of the Scots', 1297-1307
lessons.description: Scottish resistance, the First War of Scottish Independence and Edward's contested legacy.
lessons.spec_part: Part 3 — Edward I's military campaigns in Wales and Scotland
spec_bullets_covered: William Wallace and the First War of Scottish Independence from 1297 to the death of Edward I
The reputation of Edward I as 'Hammer of the Scots'
lessons.lesson_focus: William Wallace's rising 1297 and victory at Stirling Bridge, Edward's victory at Falkirk 1298 and the longbow's emergence as decisive, Wallace's capture and execution 1305, Robert Bruce's coup and coronation as King of Scots February 1306, Edward's death at Burgh-by-Sands on the way north on 7 July 1307, and an evaluation of the 'Hammer of the Scots' tomb-inscription label against the reality of an unfinished conquest.

gaps: AQA's published examiner reports for Option BB (Medieval England — Edward I) are paywalled to centres on the AQA Secure Key Materials portal, so unit-specific examiner commentary in this plan draws on (a) the publicly available 8145 mark schemes and specimen materials, (b) cross-option examiner signals shared across all four British depth study options, and (c) standard published scholarship (Morris, Prestwich, Mundill). A Unity-tier rebuild with centre access could refine the unit-specific examiner signals further.

The 2027 (Battle of Stirling Bridge) and 2028 (Acton Burnell Castle) historic environment sites are confirmed by AQA but explicitly EXCLUDED from this 2026-cycle plan. A new planner pass will be needed in 2026-27 to swap Lesson 10 for the Stirling Bridge site, and again in 2027-28 for Acton Burnell — these are date-stamped feature lessons rather than a continuous component, so the rest of the unit is stable across the three-year cycle.

Optional AQA-published 'resource pack' for Caernarfon (mentioned in the spec at line 1631) was not retrievable via web research and is distributed only to registered AQA centres. Lesson 10's content has therefore been built from open Cadw, UNESCO World Heritage and academic sources; if the AQA pack becomes available it should be cross-referenced before final ship.

Historiography section is deliberately lightweight (three positions) — the planning prompt specified 'brief contrast' rather than a full essay-length scholarly review. Content agents should not over-pad this in lesson 12's conclusion.

site_dossier.location: Caernarfon, north-west Wales (Gwynedd), at the mouth of the river Seiont where it meets the Menai Strait — strategically chosen at the seat of the former Welsh princes of Gwynedd to project English authority over the conquered heartland.
site_dossier.function: Royal fortress-palace, administrative headquarters and walled borough designed to colonise Gwynedd after Edward's victory in the second Welsh war (1282-83). Combined castle, walled town and quay as a single planned complex.
site_dossier.structure_design: Polygonal towers (not the round towers used at Conwy and Harlech), banded coloured masonry, twin-towered King's Gate facing the town, the Queen's Gate giving access to the river, and the great Eagle Tower with three turrets and walls up to 18 feet thick at the western end. Designed under master military architect Master James of St George, who oversaw the wider Edwardian castle programme.
site_dossier.symbolism: Imperial/Caesarian and Constantinopolitan iconography — banded masonry and angular towers consciously echo the walls of Constantinople and Roman imperial design, cast as a deliberate visual claim that Edward inherited the mantle of Roman emperors who had once campaigned in Britain. The choice of polygonal towers and stone bands set Caernarfon apart from the rest of Edward's Welsh ring.
site_dossier.key_dates: Construction began 1283 immediately after the second Welsh war; royal couple were housed in the Eagle Tower by Easter 1284; Edward of Caernarfon (the future Edward II) born at the castle on 25 April 1284; major damage when Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt sacked the unfinished works in 1294, then repaired and resumed; Edward I's death in 1307 left the castle still incomplete — work continued under Edward II until c.1330, total spend approximately £25,000.
site_dossier.people_connected: Edward I (commissioner and king); Queen Eleanor of Castile (in residence Easter 1284); Edward of Caernarfon (born 25 April 1284, later Edward II, presented as the first English Prince of Wales in 1301); Master James of St George (designer/master of works on the wider Edwardian Welsh castle programme); Sir Otto de Grandison (justice of north Wales); Madog ap Llywelyn (leader of the 1294-95 Welsh revolt that sacked the unfinished works).
site_dossier.links_to_depth_study: Welsh wars (Part 3): the castle was the keystone of Edward's post-1282-83 settlement and its design embodied the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) administrative shire system. Government and royal authority (Part 1): the planted English borough alongside the castle excluded Welsh inhabitants, asserting royal control through colonisation. Trade and finance (Part 2): the £25,000 build cost drove the wool tax, Italian banker loans (the Riccardi of Lucca then the Frescobaldi) and re-coinage of the late 1270s. Medieval warfare (Part 3): Caernarfon shows the late-thirteenth-century shift from motte-and-bailey to concentric and gatehouse-led design, with arrow loops, machicolations and murder holes designed for siege resistance — proven when the 1294 revolt forced rebuilding.
